utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we please have appearances, starting with the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perisic. Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution, together with Carmela Javier, Mr. Barney Thomas, Mr. Rafael La Cruz, and I'm Dan Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am coming to you, sir. I'm just having a technical problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we then have appearances for the Defence, please. Good morning, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Milos Androvic, Eadaoin O'Brien, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, who are assisting myself, I'm Gregor Guy-Smith, with Mr. Novak Lukic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am advised, Madam Sutherland, that -- or shall I address myself to you, Mr. Saxon, that the Prosecution has a preliminary issue they would like to raise before we carry on with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour. It must be a confusion that I created. I simply asked for a moment for a preliminary matter before Witness Torkildsen comes into the courtroom today, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. That being the case, then once again, Mr. Treanor, I say you do know this, but it's our duty that you are bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the Registrar could call the document that we had up on the screen yesterday that we were discussing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Somehow I don't hear you at all. You're not coming through. You're very far from the mic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slightly better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me try this and see if this improves the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Actually, the interpreters cannot hear Mr. Guy-Smith either so well. Can you speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear the interpreter clearly but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can hear the interpreter crystal clear. If I'm like this, can I be heard at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. I hear you not through the system. I hear you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hello? I feel like I'm about to sing a song or something. I don't think I can work like this necessarily. Let me try something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just pull it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me try the other microphone. If I'm speaking here, am I being heard now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's the same thing, Mr. Guy-Smith. When you're close to the microphone we can hear you, whether it's the left one or the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me try something else really quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will also try to increase our volume, although that causes a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I use this microphone here, am I heard from this position? If you give me a moment, I'll shift positions, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised by Judge Picard that if we go to channel 0, she hears you very well in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, excellent. Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just try it before you move lots. Now you don't know how to switch it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm, once again, trying to make it work so that people can hear me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the interpreters hear?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can, Your Honour. We can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Stay here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, go back. They can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Just to make sure I'm speaking from this microphone, I trust that I can be heard by the Chamber, the interpreters, Prosecution and, of course, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters say -- did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. Great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we're sorry about that inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem. Should I proceed at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have the document that we were discussing yesterday back up on the screen, and if we could at this point go to the -- I believe it's the third page, paragraph 9, is where we left off in yesterday's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We were, to refresh your recollection, Mr. Treanor, discussing a document which is the report of the Secretary-General that was issued on the 30th of May, 1992, pursuant to paragraph 4 of the Security Council Resolution 752. And going to paragraph 9, with regard to, once again, the issue at hand being the goals, as they have been discussed, of the Serbian leadership in the period of time that we've been discussing throughout your testimony, I read you the following, which is: "Given the doubts that now exist about the ability of the authorities in Belgrade to influence General Mladic, who has left JNA, efforts have been made by UNPROFOR to appeal to him directly as well as through the political leadership of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.'" Continuing: "As a result of these efforts, General Mladic agreed on 30 May 1992 to stop the bombardment of Sarajevo. While it is my hope that the shelling of the city will not be resumed, it is also clear that the emergence of General Mladic and the forces under his command as independent actors, apparently beyond the control of JNA greatly complicates the issues raised in paragraph 4 of Security Council Resolution 752 (1992)." Now, we were discussing earlier, and by that, when I say "we," I'm referring to the conversation that you were having with Ms. Sutherland, if I'm not mistaken, about this particular resolution, that 752, and with regard to the issue of the inclusion of information in your report, it's my understanding that you were not aware of this particular document. Am I correct in that regard?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The information that is contained in this particular document certainly impacts upon your analysis, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information is not particularly relevant to the subject that I was examining, which was the goals of the Serbian leadership. As I indicated in the introduction to the report, it's primarily based on their own statements and activities. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I missed something you just said. This document is primarily based on --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report is primarily based on documents relating to the activities and statements of the Serbian leadership themselves, that is, documents generated by them. This is a report under the secretary -- the Secretary-General's name. This document, in particular this paragraph, might be very interesting in a report on the perception of the UN in regards to the situation in the former Yugoslavia, but I don't regard it as particularly interesting in regard to what the Serbian leaders were doing, or thought they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony, then, the international concerns and responses to what was occurring in the region were of no import to you with regard to your preparation of the report that you've presented to us here today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not true. I examined all the resolutions of the UN Security Council. I felt they were important because, as resolutions of the Security Council, they required action, and they formed part of the international environment in which the Serbian leaders had to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also examined letters that had been sent to the Secretary-General concerning matters that were of moment at the time, did you not? As a matter of fact, you discussed one of those exhibits -- letters with us, which I think was introduced as an exhibit, and I'll try to get it pulled up in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to, if I could, paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before we go to paragraph 13, through your testimony you have discussed with us various agreements that were proposed, for example, the Vance-Owen Plan, in an attempt to resolve the difficulties that were occurring. And with that in mind, and especially in light of what you've just said to us, I'd like to read you the following: "The anomalous position of General Mladic and the forces under his command, who are subject neither to the authority of Belgrade nor to that of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, will also need to be clarified in relation to any agreement." Now, would I be accurate in saying that the international community and specifically the United Nations Security Council was interested in obtaining agreements from the parties that were involved at that time in the conflict in the region?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a negotiating process underway, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be -- we could call that an interest in obtaining an agreement, could we not? A negotiation process has, as its intent, at its conclusion, an agreement between the parties.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interest on the part of the international community in general, I think that would be fair to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So the interplay between the international community and the parties would be of interest to you, would it not, in the compilation of your report with regard to what the Bosnian Serbs and their leadership were intending to do, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "intending to do." Again, this document is something in the summer of 1992. I mean, if I was writing a full-blown history of the negotiating process during the course of the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, the perceptions of the international actors of what was going on might figure into that, but that is not the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it that it is the manner in which you define the subject of your report that defines your lack of interest in this document for purpose of its import and its inclusion in your report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I hadn't seen the document, and if I had, I would not have included it for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the considerations contained in the document would not have impacted upon your analysis with regard to what the leadership in any of the three political entities we've discussed were interested in -- actually, four. That would be the RS, right, the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The RSK, the Republika Srpska Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The SFRY and the FRY, since there were different evolutions of the last two governments and political entities; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your last response, continuing with paragraph 13, I take it that we would obtain the same information from you, which is that this is something you would not include in your report, which is: "It is considered unrealistic that the 'Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina' would be willing to place itself under the authority of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Agreement would instead need to be sought on the disarming and disbandment of this 'Army,' though this is likely to be feasible only in the context of an overall political agreement on constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you have my question in mind, which is this is again information that you would not consider to be germane, had you known of it, to be included in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This information here indicates that there is now a fifth actor to be discussed, and that's the army as an independent reality with regard to a force to be reckoned with at that time, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the opinion of whoever is writing this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the person who's writing the report is the Secretary-General, Boutros-Ghali; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he signed the report. I'm sure he didn't write it. He's responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're not denigrating his opinion by virtue of the fact that he didn't write the report, are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I'm just saying that he signed the report. I don't think he wrote it. The information came from the field, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge one way or the other as to how this report was compiled, do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not direct knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The comment that you just made in that regard with regard to whether or not he wrote the report or not, you're not suggesting in any fashion, are you, that he was retreating from the information that's contained in this report, are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that the information upon which he relied was given to him in good faith, are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, I guess my point was that the information probably came closer to the field than he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Now, he goes on in paragraph 14 to discuss what the international community could do in the event there were agreements in place, correct, starting with the language on paragraph 14: "Provided the necessary agreements were in place, international assistance could take various forms --"

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he discusses what those are. Now, I take it, again, that once again this particular kind of information, the information that's contained in paragraph 14 and the information that is contained in paragraph 15, is information that, had you known about it, would not have impacted your report or your analysis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again, it would seem to take me, at this point, especially considering the events in December of 1992, rather far from the subject matter, given the -- especially given the parameters that I was working within.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those parameters, as I recall, were time and space, or lack of time --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the lack of time and not enough space.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a subject matter and constraints of time and space. So I would not -- if I'd known about this report, I certainly would not have used this particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've now expanded from what you told us before, which is now you've indicated there was another issue which is the subject matter itself, which is something you did not discuss with us yesterday in terms of what your constraints were. And since this report is dealing directly with not only a resolution, that being 752, that you did -- that you did include in your report, but also deals with, directly, observations that are being made about how the international community and specifically the United Nations is going to respond to issues concerning leadership, this would be information that is contained within the subject matter that your report addresses, would it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can, again, quote from the introduction of the report: "The focus is on the goals of the Serbian leaders and the extent to which they achieve them." That's in paragraph 4. I don't consider that in a 60-page or, whatever it is, 75-page report on that particular subject that this material would warrant consideration. I would be the first to admit that there are -- and I would be the first to be able to direct the Court to dozens, indeed hundreds of documents that would be use -- might be useful to consider in any examination of the situation between 1991 and 1995 as it related to the international negotiations, the international community's involvement therein, and indeed the actions, activities, and goals of all the parties to the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "the goals of all the parties to the conflicts," you, of course, include in that not only the international community but the Bosnian Serb leadership, as you have collectively identified this group; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb -- yes, but also the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The other parties being?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Muslims, the Government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And since you've now identified for us at least in one respect that there are hundreds of other documents, your determination of which documents should have been used, included in the report, and should not have been used or were not used because you did not deem them to be relevant is something, which you discussed with us yesterday, is based upon a criteria that you have within your own thought processes; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said if one was given full consideration to all the action -- all those actions and activities that I described between 1991 and 1995, there would be a very vast material. This report is confined to the subject matter that I just specified. Within the constraints that I was operating within, I produced what I hoped was a report, including the -- and I believe includes the most relevant documents to the consideration of that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, could I have the document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document ID001-449 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D6, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And finally, just so we're clear with regard to the general issue of your report and the extent to which you commented or relied on any statements made by the United Nations Security Council President, I believe, if I'm not mistaken, you made comments and specifically referred to them in paragraphs 180, 183, 184, 206, 223, 225, 227, 232, and 233. Do you take my word for that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's mention of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The President or the Secretary-General, you make mention in those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I'd like to turn our attention, if we could, to -- I believe it's the meeting that was held on the 9th of January, 1993, which is P205.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you calling P205?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm calling P205 up at this time, although I need to double-check something, which is P205 as it presently exists, I believe, may only be a couple of pages as opposed to the entire document. So could I call up 65 ter 6620.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, 6620 is Exhibit P205.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In its entirety?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. Pages 71 and 92 of the English and page 70, 95, and 96 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to call up, as I understand it, the entire document, and perhaps I'm calling up the wrong document. But when I had the 65 ter list -- and perhaps we can get some initial help from the Prosecution, if they would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's the correct Rule 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do I get the entire document when I pull up that particular -- when I ask you to pull up that particular 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Great. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask for extra microphones to be switched off, please. Audibility is reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In a minute we'll have the English page up on the screen, but while we're waiting, this particular meeting was, as you've discussed with us, "The Enlarged Session of the Council for Reconciliation of the Stands on State Politics"; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in this meeting there were quite a large number of participants, were there not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there were participants from not only FRY representatives, but there were representatives from the Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina; true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if people from Krajina were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If you turn to the -- page 2 in the English, and, I believe, it's also page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you could enlarge it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does a review of that page refresh your recollection as to whether or not there were representatives from Republika Srpska Krajina there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the general purpose of this meeting was to discuss what was occurring at the time in Geneva and the negotiations in Geneva; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the purposes of the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, turning to page 3 in the English and page 3 also in the B/C/S, looking at the very beginning paragraph where Mr. Cosic indicates what the topics are to be discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the topic to be discussed -- the purpose of the meeting was to agree on our stance on the negotiations in Geneva; true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's number 1. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at this meeting, what was occurring, at least initially, was that a report was being made with regard to the possible scenarios of course work or the possible manners in which some form of agreement could be reached; right? And if the --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally they were discussing the situation, the status of negotiations in Geneva. These are the Vance-Owen negotiations and how to proceed with the next meeting, which was due to take place at this point. They were stranded in Belgrade because of the weather in Geneva or something, so they had a meeting while they were waiting to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, they were talking about very specific proposals and very specific issues with regard to what was occurring in Geneva; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I mean, it wasn't a general about, What should we do next, but rather, it was a very specific discussion with regard to the context in which the Geneva Conference was being guided by Lord Owen; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And they discussed their strategy in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And they discussed before their strategy or the goals that they had for this particular conference, they discussed what the international community and specifically what Lord Owen believed could occur and could not occur; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been discussion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, turning to page 3, let's see whether or not that's of any assistance in terms of whether or not there may have been any such discussion. This is a continuation from page 2 where Mr. Cosic is saying that there are three separate scenarios that might be played out, and I'm sure that's what you were talking about when you're dealing with the strategies that they were discussing in their meeting.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "All sides might accept the key elements --" well, I'm not going to read them. The three of them are there. We can all see them; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, and then he specifically discusses what will happen -- I'm sorry. He specifically discusses that the Serbian side has been given diplomatic warnings by Lord Owen in the event that certain things don't happen; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For example, if there is -- "firstly, the international community will not accept the status of 'a state within a state.'" So there was clearly a discussion about what the nature of those negotiations were and how the leadership should not only respond to them, but what the problems were that they were going to faced in this agreement process; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was the purpose of this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of this portion of the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during this meeting, and by the "meeting," I'm referring to the meeting on the 6th of January -- I'm sorry, the 9th of January, one of the things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the speaker that you were referring to, I think, is Zivota Panic, not Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You know what? I think you may well be right. I think they may have moved on to Mr. Panic. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during the course of -- during the course of this discussion, various of the individuals who were present stood up and discussed various aspects of how they should respond to the international community's demands and perception of how the agreement should go; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they would like to see things go, perhaps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, how they would like to see things go. And in that they also discussed issues concerning constitution; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, Mr. Jovanovic, and referring --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have page - hopefully I'll do this properly - page 27 of the English and 25 of the Serbian up. Going to the very top of the page, the paragraph that starts with the words "First of all ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He says: "First of all, based on the existing Constitution --" Now, what constitution would that be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I would have to examine the whole passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's do that. "... we should persistently fight for reaffirmation of the principle of constitutionality. As far as we could understand, it is not possible to insert it into the text. There are logical consequences that are coming out of it. Constitutionality means nation-building qualities; to have them means to have inalienable right to self-determination." Here it says: "The unalienable right to self-determination means also the right to state organisation without right to secession. Therefore, 'a state within the state' is not impossible, and there is not small numbers of such examples in the world. Still, the state, peace and stability, as well as interests of other countries has not been brought into question." Now, here Mr. Jovanovic is discussing a fundamental aspect of what one of the important considerations is at the Geneva Conference and specifically one of the matters that Lord Owen has suggested is not possible, and he's making a statement, is he not, and one might say a well-reasoned statement, in terms of his analysis that there is a possibility to have this particular kind of a political entity and that perhaps Mr. Owen's analysis is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the -- well, in simplest terms, yes, I think we discussed some of those -- that issue yesterday, about the idea of there being three entities within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And -- thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the way, I would check the translation of this. It could be correct, but when he says "the right to self-determination means also the right to state organisation without right to secession," I would check that. That might be correct, but usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. Treanor, as you're reading the document, you can also see it in B/C/S, and looking at it in B/C/S, are you indicating that as far as you're concerned, based upon your understanding of the language, that there's a discrepancy --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- or are you conjecturing with regard to the manner in which the individuals have done their job? I'm just asking the question because I'm not sure what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that that be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that page. I'm seeing page 24. This is apparently on page 25 of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, is this a final CLSS translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems not to be. It says "OTP DVU," so we take your suggestion in hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if page 25 could be put on the screen, which would correlate with the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I thought we had that up. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we do that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what it says. It says "without." Sorry for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't hear you, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you repeat yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "without." I'm sorry if I caused any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to page 34 of the B/C/S and -- I'm sorry, I believe it's 36 of the English. And on the previous page, so we can identify the speaker, the speaker now is Milosevic, and I'd like to go to the top of the page, the very first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And we've had a fair amount of discussion about strategic goals, and with that in mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do we have the proper page up? I think it's 34 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm noting that the B/C/S needs to go on one more page to be -- correlate with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just want to wait until we have the B/C/S page up, in case you have any concerns about the language being used. Mr. Milosevic says, with in mind with the discussion that we've had about strategic goals: "I think that we should not swear now on strategic goals. They are clear. There is no person sitting at this desk that does not share that opinion. Our strategic goal is that the Serbian people in Balkan should be free and have equal rights. Freedom and equal rights of the Serbian people in Balkan then can include all possibilities for them to be fully recognised and to accomplish their interests. We can draw a line there at the goals. Since all the speeches were about that; it is clear, and we agree with it. If we wonder how - it is less important to me through how many institutional decisions and phases the goal is to be achieved, but it is more important to know how many people have to die for that goal and whether it is necessary." And then he goes on to say: "I am sure that we absolutely have not used the space that we have available for negotiations." Now, I see that you're looking back and forth between the two, so I want to make sure that, first of all --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought you were, and I don't mean to be presumptuous about what you were doing. Now, that particular statement, with regard to the information that you have presented to us here, do you believe that that particular statement as it specifically uses the terminology "strategic goals" is something that is of relevance and importance to have been included in your report, number 1? Is that of importance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean the mention here of strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The statement that he makes with regard to a definition of what he, Milosevic, deems the strategic goals to be - the equal rights and freedom of the people.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that particular idea is something that he had expressed earlier and already figured in the report. I think what I did include in the report was something else --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this is --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I thought that was the important thing from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this is a slightly different definition of strategic goals than which you have presented to us, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is Mr. Milosevic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'm asking you a question. Please give me an answer yes or no, and then you can explain it. This is a slightly different definition of strategic goals from that which you have given us, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are different strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 38 of the English and of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, these could well be different goals. It's not entirely clear. I think he's speaking on -- from his point of view, he's certainly not referring to the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's clear that he's referring to the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, with regard to who this speaker is, this is one of the individuals who was, in your estimation, part of the leadership which your report concerned between 1990 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that's Mr. Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And during --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know if I gave you the appropriate page in B/C/S. If I did not, I apologise. I believe it's 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is Milosevic continuing and talking about an issue that you mentioned earlier on, which is another point that was of some importance to everyone's determination, specifically to a determination of how you would define the state. And Mr. Milosevic indicates -- I'm sorry, I'm going to read from -- starting on page 37 of the English. I do apologise. He says: "All right. Let us make it be so that the first principle would say that 'Bosnia and Herzegovina is' - and then going to the language we have right now - is decentralized state made of three constitutive peoples in organized provinces with high level of exercise of power, so that is something what they do accept."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, are you reading anything from what we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see what's happened here. Could we please have for but a moment page 37 of the English. Going to the very bottom of the page, last paragraph, the very last -- the very last sentence, referring to the conversation that he had with Cyrus Vance, quote, referring to Cyrus Vance: "All right, let us make it be so that the first principle would say that 'Bosnia and Herzegovina is ...'" and then if we could, Madam Registrar, go to the next page in English and remain on the same page in B/C/S, and then go to the very top of the page. "'... decentralised state made of three constitutive peoples and organised provinces with high level of exercise of power.' So that is something what they do accept." And he is referring to Cyrus Vance accepting an idea, which he then continues to explain. "They have not used terms 'composite' or 'unitary;' they just said decentralised state of three constitutive peoples.' If that term - three constitutive peoples - would be established as the first principle, then it automatically comes to the right to self-determination. If it is about constitutive people, then what else it could be but that the people that have right to self-determination, which is contained in the definition itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems from this, at least in terms of his analysis in the discussion that he is having with the leadership at the time, and by "leadership," I mean the leadership of RS, RSK, FRY, that there is here the ability to obtain the goal, the strategic goal, that we were just referring to a moment ago. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't know that that's -- the two passages are directly related. I mean, what he's discussing here, they are discussing a draft of constitutional principles, I believe it was called, which had eight or nine points which had been drawn up in Geneva, and they were going to be the subject of further discussion in Geneva, and so they're going over the current draft and talking about changes in the draft. And he's emphasising that the idea of the three constituent or constituted peoples has been accepted, which, I think, is something we've discussed here, and that they would therefore have the right to self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I'm sorry. This is in Bosnia, of course. This is restricted to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the suggestion made but a few moments earlier with regard to the strategic goal of freedom and equality, or equal rights, in his estimation, is being met through the agreement process that is going on at that time? Be it a draft or be it a final document, this is a positive, a positive step towards peace.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He sees this -- he would see what he's describing here as a positive step toward that particular goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Then there's further discussion, still again with regard to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have page 58 of the English and 56 of the B/C/S. The speaker has changed, and for purposes of identification, the speaker can be found at page 57. This is Mr. Stojanovic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Incidentally, who was Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think he was one of the advisors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He'd be identified on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the first page when it says, "he was the Special Advisor to the President;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which president?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would have been Cosic, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And looking at the second paragraph in English, in talking about, once again, a way of discussing at the conference how to formulate this agreement, he says: "I am returning to a formula that I have been representing for a long time because it would be impossible for an American to refuse calling it: 'The United States of Bosnia and Herzegovina.' It would mean that three states exist. Let us start from that term. Starting from that term, let us create and make stronger all the confederal elements, which means not only three constitutive principles but also three states. It means that we should combine the principle of territorial unification with the principle of consensus, whereby it would not only be the question of territory but also of the function." Now, here it seems that he's suggesting something that we were talking about yesterday, which is a return to a federalised system with three, shall we say, states, similar to what we discussed when we were talking about the United States of America and the 50 states, as compared to the former Yugoslavia with the six republics. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's discussing here the idea of making the confederal elements stronger. We've seen in some of the documents that were presented during my testimony that Mr. Milosevic and the Serbian leaders in general made a strong distinction between a confederation and a federation. He said that a confederation was not a state, and here he's referring to strengthening the confederal elements in the Bosnian constitution so that there would be three states.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed so. And then he goes on to define, does he not, what the relationship of those three states would be to each other?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The constitutional principles that were under discussion did that, which were eventually accepted by all parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the leadership at this time internally was discussing a methodology and a conceptual understanding of how to define the political inter-relationship between the parties that was ultimately accepted. And when you say "ultimately accepted," do I understand you to mean at the time of the signing of Dayton?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As mentioned in my report, there were two packages of documents signed, one at the end of January 1993 and then another package in the end of March 1993, which consisted of, I believe, the constitutional principles, a transitional agreement, and a map. Eventually, meaning by the end of March, all parties had signed off on all those documents, except the Bosnian Serb leadership had not signed the map, and that got to be the central issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with your last explanation in mind, turning to page 104 of the English and 102 of the B/C/S, if we could, please. Once again, Stojanovic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second full paragraph -- I'm sorry, if we could go under to where Stojanovic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going to his second point, he now is discussing his -- what he believes could be the appropriate tactics to be used during the negotiation and compromising process, and he says: "Second, if we are going for negotiations and compromising, even in this maximal variant where things will be sharpened to a razor edge, then we would have to discuss tactics. The best tactics would be to take some western example to support each proposal for improvement. For an example, we can take the internal organisation of the USA as an example for the United States of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that case they cannot say that there cannot be such a state if the USA is such a state. In some other case, where it suits us, we can refer to West-German Constitution. We can use Canada as an appropriate example due to the ethnical problems that they have. We can even involve Russia, since Russia has federal relations between the Republics and Autonomous Provinces, et cetera." Now, in that statement, he is embodying a series of concepts with regard to what would be matters to discuss on the table how best to reach an agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regard to the constitutional principles, apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have all of those pages admitted, and at the conclusion, at the break, we'll meet with the registrar, if that's appropriate, and make sure that we have the right pages both in B/C/S and English so that they are, whatever the word it is they used, in terms of -- "linked" is what they say. Since sometimes I may have called it the wrong page, unless it's been taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All those pages that were referred to in P205, Exhibit P205, are admitted into evidence as Defence exhibits. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D7, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to move to another area if I could, please, which is -- which is you mentioned earlier that Celeketic was at one point, I believe, the head of the army for the SVK.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I saw a document on that dated February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who appointed him? Was that done through the Assembly process, as we discussed, as occurred with Mr. Mladic, or did that occur in a different fashion with a direct appointment by the president?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was appointed by the -- well, my recollection -- from recollection, he was appointed by Milan Martic, who was the new president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before Martic, who was the President of the SVK?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And under Goran Hadzic, the head of the army was somewhat different than Celeketic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure who Celeketic replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've told us that the constitution of the SVK and the constitution of the RS were relatively similar in nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I have a transcript page reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. That will take me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the question, instead of saying "you told us," let me ask you the question: Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe so. In it regards what it says about the command of the army, I think they are fairly similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go, and I think we still need to do this in closed session, and it will take but a moment, but if can we go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into closed session. 24 [Closed session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is one document that we have under seal, which is P215, which is entitled "The Directive for the use of the Yugoslav Army, Republika Srpska, and Army of Serbian Krajina, dated 14th of November, 1993." And I have a couple of questions with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it -- you've had a chance to go through this document, have you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is a plan of what the response could be in the event that certain conditions take place; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. This is not -- this is not a -- this is not what we call a proactive plan, but rather a defensive plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A contingency plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by "contingency," the contingency plan involves what would occur if various aggressors, as it's put in terms of the plan itself, effected attacks; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the basic idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And did this plan, to your knowledge, require legislation of any sort?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether this plan ever took effect?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume it came into effect immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by that you mean that the idea came into effect immediately?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by that I mean that should that contingency develop immediately, the directive would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your understanding from your review of this that this was a -- this was a turnkey plan. And by that I mean -- you understand what I mean by "a turnkey plan"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was ready to go?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm done with this particular document, and if we could -- this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, you don't have any specific page from this document that you want to tender into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, not based upon what the gentleman has said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is removed from the screen. May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll now take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Quite briefly, right before we start, I've been informed that I need to make two corrections to the transcript where I misspoke myself on page 30, at lines 14 and 19, apparently I said "VSK," and I should have said "RSK," and I apologise for doing that. At page 30, line 14, it should be "RSK" and at page 30, line 19, it should be "RSK."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 14 and 19. 15, I'm sorry. I said "VSK ,"and it should be "RSK" at line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then at line 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Line 20. Maybe my synchronisation skills will get better as time goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I would now like to call up, if we could, P217, which is the 20th session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 15th of April, 1994. I'm sorry, once again, this is going to be partial because of the situation which we're in, so I need to have 65 ter number 6639.01. Before we go any further, I have been requested by our client to have this entire document admitted. It is 46 pages long, and I am aware of the guidelines that we have. I'm going to be referring to a number of pages within the document, and what I would propose is that I do that which we have done in the rules that we are following and at the conclusion the Chamber can make a determination as to whether or not it would be appropriate to have the entire document in or proceed along the lines that we have been proceeding. But it would be our request to have at the conclusion this entire document in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are there any special reasons that can be advanced at this stage for the entire document to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from -- apart from specific requests made by Mr. Perisic and the generalised concern about notions of completeness, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Perisic give you any reason why he wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he believes that this document should be -- should be admitted in its entirety so that the Chamber has the full context and the "give and take" of the information that's contained within the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. We'll consider that at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I'd like to direct your attention to the third page of the document in English, which I believe to be the second page of the document in B/C/S, but I could be incorrect. But that's what I believe it to be. I don't know if we have the B/C/S up yet, but I'll begin -- yes, it is up. I will begin the discussion. Now, this is a meeting which concerns itself with the Republic of FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a FRY document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And FRY, as you've told us before, is one of the, shall we say, republics that was created after the -- or during the dissolution of the breakup of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in regards to the issue of FRY, at that time in 1994 the President of FRY was a Mr. Lilic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he was also the President of the Supreme Defence Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Perisic had been appointed by Lilic sometime in 1993, I believe in August of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when Perisic was appointed, he was appointed under the laws of the constitution and the laws of the army; correct? And that's of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would have been appointed under whatever legislative was operative at the time. I think the new law on the Army of Yugoslavia only came into effect later in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Perisic was subordinate to -- under the law, he was subordinate to Lilic; correct? He was the president.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the 20th session, and now I'm directing your attention to the page which is up on the screen, Mr. Perisic essentially begins this session to discuss what the situation is with regard to FRY; correct? And he says: "This is more than our soldiers' view of the political solution of the crisis in this region. Later I would like to tell you about our concrete measures undertaken and the danger for the SR/Federal Republic/of Yugoslavia/FRY."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in this session which you have analysed and you have reviewed, Mr. Perisic discusses in this session measures that need to be taken or should be taken in order to protect the security of FRY; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, he focuses quite specifically in that regard, and directing your attention to page 9, which is, if I'm correct, the middle -- starts in the middle of page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not seeing it yet; 9 in the English, 6 in the B/C/S. Yes. And going to the third paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before this, he has discussed what is, in his view as the Chief of Staff of FRY, occurring in the region militarily, which he's reporting to the Supreme Defence Council about, and then he says: "In order to prevent surprise and not provoke them by anything, we have undertaken the following measures: we've stepped up security at the borders to Albania, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina; we have engaged a larger number of men along the axes and sent units for in-depth security of the border." And there, the security of the border that he's referring to is the border of FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: His concern here, then, his stated concern here, as a military man, is to protect the sanctity of that particular region, and by "that particular region," I mean the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's concerned with the security of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And he goes on in the next paragraph to say that again, he is -- "he" meaning the army, has put "air force and anti-aircraft units into the state of combat alert. In case of escalation of danger, we have planned that," and then he names them, "PVO/anti-aircraft defence units would come out to the eastern Republic of Serbian Krajina border with Croatia and Bosnia in order to protect the bridges and prevent," and there's a document that I have in English, there's a question mark with regard to the next word which says "possible, violation of our territory." So the balance of that sentence would either read "prevent violation of our territory" or "prevent the possible violation of our territory." And this may be a point where you might like to take at it in the original and see whether you discern a difference between the two. Do you see a difference there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "... in order to protect the bridges and prevent possible violation of our territory."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- well, eventual violation. But it's "violation of our territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, all right. In any event, the underlying -- the underlying --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a funny word that's being used there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the translator does think so, too, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In any event, the idea here is that he is doing that which is what a person in his position, commander of the army, should be doing, which is considering how best to protect his borders.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he's reporting that to those that he answers to, those that are in authority over him; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He goes on to discuss further -- further ideas of how best to deploy or not deploy various troops and individuals on the next pages, which I will not go into, and ultimately he concludes his discussion, if we could have page 15, please, which I believe -- page 15 in the English -- which is B/C/S, the last paragraph on page 10, and then I think we'll have to go over to page 11, but I'm not absolutely positive. I'm just dealing with the one point which is the Perisic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think page 15 is under seal, so you will have to go to the under-seal exhibit and go into --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, and thank you so much for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the redacted version of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you for the -- my concern is with the top of the page, so we may be in a position to proceed. I'm only going for the last comment made by Mr. Perisic which has not been redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you want to continue with this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means, carry on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we're okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you don't need private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And finally he concludes here by saying: "I presented our line of reasoning in the worst possible case. I think we should prepare for it hoping that it won't happen. We would be very happy if it didn't. But these are our calculations of what could befall us in the worst case of escalation of the conflict in this region, while we are doing everything to prevent it." And there what he was referring to is the security of the borders of the FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even more generally, involvement of -- yes, having the conflict brought in -- to the territory of FRY, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that, as a matter of fact, is something that had not occurred. The conflict had not been brought into the territory of FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I am finished with that particular document, and depending on the Chamber's view, would either rule for the admission of the entire document or for admission of the pages, whatever the Chamber deems appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The entire document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe that document should be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D8, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does that work?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that the unredacted version should be admitted in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we're in total agreement here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's fine. I was admitting the document that was on display.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but what was on the screen was the redacted version, so we would seek to have the -- if the Defence want the total of the 20th session of the SDC into evidence, we would -- it's our submission that the entire unredacted version should be put into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that we have no disagreement here, and I believe that because one was redacted and one was unredacted, and the unredacted one, I believe, is 65 ter number 6639 -- Carmela, is that .01? Thank you. .01, 6639.01 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So 06639 is the unredacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. If we could have 06639, which is the unredacted version, admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hope I'm saying the right thing at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, may I just clarify our position. The only -- the pages that are protected pursuant to a court order are from page 11, paragraph 3 on page 11, onwards, so they're the only ones that we would seek to be under seal. The other -- the first eleven pages can be a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam, how is that practical? Is that practically possible? This is one document. Some pages are under seal; others are not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have a solution, Your Honour. The redacted exhibit, which is P217, certain pages of that were admitted through my examination of Mr. Treanor. If the whole lot of the unredacted version is in evidence and then we have the unredacted version, which is 06639, under seal, we achieve the same -- we achieve the same balance, because we have an exhibit that has the unredacted pages, and that's a public exhibit, and then we have the other exhibit which is under seal and that's the entirety of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. You have referred to the pages that you wanted to refer to and you have tendered them into evidence as P217, so the whole document that is now being tendered by the Defence can go entirely in, under seal, and anybody who wants to cross-check can cross-check. I just don't think we should now at this stage admit publicly the pages that were referred to by the Defence and then admit under seal the entire document and still have P217. This is just burdening the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, what I'm saying is that under P217, only the pages I took Mr. Treanor to, according to Your Honours' ruling that we don't put in the entire documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So now that the situation's changed in relation to this particular document, we would seek to have the entire exhibit -- the Rule 65 ter number 06639.01, which at the moment only has specific pages, but if that whole exhibit which is the unredacted version of those -- that session of the 20th session of the SDC, if that's a public exhibit, and then we have this other unredacted version under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying the Chamber is not inclined to do. It is not inclined to admit one document three times over. I don't see why, if we already have P217, we can't just have the rest of the document or the entire document as per the request of the Defence admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But the public don't get to see the information, Your Honour. The Defence have asked for the whole exhibit to be put in, and we've agreed with that on the proviso that the public are entitled to see what is not redacted from that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you know what --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we admit P217, which is just some pages of the document, then the public doesn't see the rest of the document. You didn't intend to do that. The Prosecution wants to -- wanted to admit the entire redacted document. You said no, you don't want the entire redacted document, you want the entire document unredacted. Now, are you saying simply because now the Defence wanted to have admitted the redacted part in its entirety, now you want that whole redacted part made public?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding -- if I understood you well just then, you said that the Defence wanted the whole of the redacted version admitted, but it's not my understanding of what they want. They want the whole session admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour. Rather than pedaling through yoghurt if the Prosecution and the Defence can get together at the break, we'll take a look at the status of these exhibits, and we'll come back to the Chamber with an appropriate solution, if a solution there need be, and I believe there's some confusion here. So if we could just move on at this point in time, I promise you we'll get the matter resolved, and I'm sure it'll be resolved to the satisfaction of all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the admission of this document is deferred pending the negotiations between the parties. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. If we could have 65 ter 6606 brought forth, some of those pages have been previously admitted as P230.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt again. It was my understanding that the Defence were to provide a list of all the exhibits that they were going to use with each witness at the end of the examination-in-chief. We were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- we were provided -- we were advised in the middle of Mr. Treanor's cross-examination yesterday of the documents that had been released into e-court, and my colleague said that that was an oversight on his behalf for not telling the Prosecution that they had released the documents earlier. But we still have not been provided with a list of all of these documents, and even though they're Rule 65 ter numbers and we have access to the documents, we should still have a list of the exhibits that they intend to use through Mr. Treanor and with each witness, and I would ask that you direct the Defence to do that from this point on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll take that -- we'll take that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could know now the exhibits that you intend -- any other additional exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 65 ter 6606, which was previously -- pages of which were previously admitted as Exhibit P230 which would --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are there additional exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- which would not be the case had the entire document been admitted. After this discussion there will be no further documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- of which the Prosecution is not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but the Defence missed the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, the Defence has not missed the point at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
