utterances.text: We have all the documents because they are Rule 65 ter documents, but we're supposed to be provided with a list of the exhibits they're going to use with this witness, whether they're 65 ter exhibits or they're new exhibits they're uploading and releasing to us in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is simply not a problem. The point was taken. The point was understood, specifically understood. And I promise you, Your Honour, if I can get to the next question and the question after that, you will see precisely why I've said what I've said. There's no mystery going on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot wait for your next question before the Court makes a ruling. There's a request for a ruling to be made --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you have taken the point, I understand, and can I just make the ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm saying I'm taking it even further than I've taken the point. I'm more than happy to agree with what the Prosecution has said, and I welcome a ruling that precisely indicates what the Prosecution has asked for. So the Chamber is fully aware of what my position is and what Mr. Lukic's position is, we have no difficulty at all with the proposal, and we are more than happy to abide by such an order if you choose to impose such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. If we could have, I believe it's page 7 of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, for my own clarification, you've called for 65 ter 06606 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want the entire document or do you want P230?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I want the entire document at this time. I actually want only one page of this document because the Prosecution chose not to introduce the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is which, Mr. Guy-Smith? Do you want the entire document, or do you want one page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want one page. I want page 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- of the English, which is, I believe, page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we have page 6 of 65 ter 06606, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could go down to the bottom of the page. Excellent. And I'm going to start with, really, the very last -- the last paragraph which is a notation of what Milosevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this particular information is not -- is not a verbatim of what was said, but rather notes of a meeting that was had; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And you had discussed with us, I believe, certain aspects of this particular document, P230. This document, of which certain pages were introduced which were P230, and I'm going now to the page before that which you found to be relevant. This is page 6 of the English, and we had been discussing page 7 before. And at the bottom, Milosevic says that: "We did not have time for such tactics and that we should not be out-manoeuvre one another." And that "out-manoeuvring" he's talking about, there is an out-manoeuvring as between Karadzic's position and Milosevic's position; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to examine that, but I'll accept your characterization.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, he says -- the note says that Milosevic went on to say: "Now we must gain as much as possible. To illustrate that negotiations with international mediators have not been easy, President Milosevic mentioned the fact that, in order to secure the Republika Srpska international legitimacy and rights equal to those of the Croatian-Muslim federation, he fought for six months for the acceptance of just one word: 'equal'"; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, although it says negotiate -- "to illustrate that negotiations with international mediators have not been easy." I think you might have said "internal."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. So he is expressing there the view that what he had been striving for, one of the members of, as you call it, a Serbian leadership, what he'd been striving for for some period of time is a matter that we've discussed, as a matter of fact, earlier today, that being freedom and equality, is something that took, just for the one particular idea, that of equality, took six months to get through with the international negotiators; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the negotiations about Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When was Dayton signed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was kind of a two-stage process. I think there was something signed preliminarily at the end of November 1995 and then a more formal signing in Paris in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And upon the signing of Dayton, that terminated the conflict in the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- yes, it had already been terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It had already been terminated.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Broadly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a point on that page that came up. The Defence said that the Prosecution chose not to tender that page into evidence. It's part of Exhibit P230, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, did you deliberately not tender that page, or is it just an oversight?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, no, I meant to tender the page. I was certainly not an oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then page 6 of P230 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm informed -- excuse me, I'm sorry. I'm informed that at page 36, line 2, the answer by Mr. Treanor was put as a question, so it should be an A and not a Q.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that you've just made D7 is already part of Exhibit P230. That was my point, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document I've just made D7 or D8?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: D8. The Defence misstated the record when they said that the Prosecution chose not to admit this page. It was admitted already as Exhibit D -- P230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that because the document that I have that was supplied to me indicates that the passage that I read is on page 6 of the English translation and not on page 7, so I cannot confirm that. I can confirm that page 6, which is where -- the page that I brought up on the English translation that I'm reading, as I'm looking at it right now, that's page 6 on the bottom of the page, and that information was not given. And that Ms. Sutherland, at --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold on, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland at page 1255, line 10, asked for pages 1 and 7 of the English translation be admitted, and that's at line 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour. I was advised that it was part of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I take responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you were asked by the Defence, and this is to paraphrase the Defence question, whether from 1990 -- and this is at transcript page 1319, whether from 1992 to 1995 the driving goal of the Serbian leadership was to obtain equality and protection for the Serbs through the formation of a single state or a number of states. Given the documentation that you have reviewed, was the goal of the formation of a single Serb state conceived or formulated in 1992 or earlier?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At what point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the SFRY was a single state in which all the Serbs lived. That was formed in 1945 or even 1943.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But the goals of the formation of a single Serb state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. You're talking about the SFRY, not the FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SFRY, yes. That was a state in which all Serbs lived. Now, the issue -- that issue of a state in which all Serbs live came up again when the SFRY dissolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But we're talking about the goal of the leadership -- of the Serb leadership during this period of 1990 to 1995, when this breakup of the former Yugoslavia took place, sir. We're not talking about the formation of the SFRY in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Within the context of the breakup of the SFRY, we saw that formulated in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but then -- thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Therefore, the goal of creating a single Serb state out of the territories of the former Yugoslavia that the Serbian leaders thought were rightfully theirs, a reaction to the policies of Alija Izetbegovic, as the Defence seem to suggest at transcript page 1304, lines 14 to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- and 20 to 23.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the idea of -- that all Serbs -- the desire that all Serbs should live within the state -- within one state had little to do with anything that Alija Izetbegovic may or may not have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your report at paragraph 25, and that's Rule 65 ter exhibit 06646.01, you discuss a platform on the future of the Yugoslav community by Izetbegovic and the Macedonian president Gregorov dating from the beginning of June 1991. Do you recall what position Izetbegovic took in that proposal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just get certainty before the answer is given. Is 65 ter 06601 an exhibit? Has it been admitted into evidence as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The number that you just read out, Your Honour, isn't the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the correct number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 06646.01. And it's not an exhibit as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does that arise from the cross-examination, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's his report, and it arises from cross-examination because the Defence -- I read out the page numbers in relation to the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe before you make reference to that 65 ter document, give us the background of how it becomes relevant by putting questions to the witness. Let's see how they relate to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said, as the Defence suggested at transcript page 1304, lines 14 to 18 and 20 to 23, the Defence was suggesting to Mr. Treanor that the goal of creating a single Serb state out of the territories of the former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was as a result of Izetbegovic's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and he answered that question comprehensively by saying no, it had nothing to do with anything Izetbegovic had said or done, something to that effect. I thought he had answered you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you still want to pursue it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, at transcript page 1307, line 16, counsel asked you about the internal borders in the SFRY. Based on your research and on your report, who opened up the question of internal borders in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you mean by "opening up the question." The republics that wanted to secede wanted to keep the borders that they had within the SFRY. The Serbs regarded those and said that they regarded those as internal administrative borders and that they could be -- could be subject to revision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's referred to in your report at paragraph 15 -- no, Exhibit P150. What you just referred to then, is that part of the Milosevic speech, which is Exhibit P150, or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. He referred to that in one of the speeches we saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you just said in relation to the position of all the other Yugoslav republics, that they wanted to keep the borders that they had within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the position of the international community, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe their position was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if we could have a time period of the position of the international community now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yesterday, you referred to the Badinter opinion. If I can take you to page 149 of your report --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 149, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, what was the position of the international community?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, the position taken was that the borders could be changed but only by agreement and not by force. At this particular time in -- starting in January, member states of the EC started recognising the independence of some of the republics, notably Slovenia and Croatia, within the borders that they had had within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic. At page -- transcript page 1297, it was suggested to you that Slobodan Milosevic's speeches were, and I quote, "that he was constantly from, I believe as you said, from the end of 1991 forward pressing for some kind of peace settlement." Besides the Milosevic speech in July 1991, which is P153, and then the reference in April 1993 of the 29th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly where peace again was raised, do you recall anywhere in your report or anywhere in your testimony of Milosevic advocating for peace in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I can't recall anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would have thought that if there is any part -- any place in his report where he refers to Milosevic advocating peace, you can direct his attention to that part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I have reviewed the report, and I do not find any cite to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is it the case that Milosevic was advocating peace in April 1993 because the Serbs had occupied at that stage, the Bosnian Serbs, over 70 per cent of the territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not he's in a position to answer that question. I think it's outside the purview of his expertise, the reason why he's advocating peace, in terms of the way the question's being phrased. I think that's a conclusion, if it's to be drawn at all, to be drawn by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By the end of 1992, how much territory was occupied by the Bosnian Serbs in BH?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 70 per cent, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you've given evidence earlier that -- and taken the Trial Chamber to different sessions of -- the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions and the SDC sessions, showing that the FRY leadership stated at those sessions that they wanted the Bosnian Serbs to accept the peace agreement or the peace plan because they'd got what they wanted. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me clarify. You said "they got what they wanted." I think this is an important point that has come up tangentially. Who is "they," and what did they want? We've seen reference -- numerous references to the Bosnian Serb strategic goals. Those were goals adopted by the Bosnian Serb Assembly within the framework of the war, if you will, that was going on within Bosnia at that time. The leadership in Belgrade was aware of these goals and may not have entirely agreed with them. They had their own goals, one of which was -- or among which were not necessarily the achievement of all the Bosnian Serbs' strategic goals to the extent that the Bosnian Serbs might have liked. There came a point in time, certainly by the beginning of 1993, that Mr. Milosevic felt that enough had been achieved in the war to warrant ending the war and get confirmation of what had been achieved by way of recognition of the territory and the recognition of a Bosnian Serb entity in Bosnia in a fashion similar to what had happened in Croatia the year before, in early 1992, when he felt that enough had been achieved and it was time to get it recognised. Of course the Croatian Serbian leadership objected to that, and he ran into difficulties with the Bosnian Serb leadership later. He was very anxious to achieve the goal of getting that entity in Bosnia recognised, on the one hand, and on the other, his country was suffering under sanctions and was also making large outlays in connection with the conflict in Bosnia, and he wished to relieve his country of those burdens, as well as he stated on a number of occasions, to save lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from a review of the documents, even though it was -- it may have been the position that the FRY leadership wasn't always in agreement or wanted the Bosnian Serbs to accept the -- what was being put on the negotiating table, that the Bosnian Serbs didn't want to do that. While there may have been some disagreements, did they continue to support financially and materially until the end of the war the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That certainly is outside of the cross-examination and also is, as a matter of fact, outside of the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any questions? Any questions? Thank you very much, Mr. Treanor. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You may now be -- you are now excused, and you may stand down. Thank you once again for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope I've been able to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender into evidence Mr. Treanor's CV and his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we deal with that once he has left? Mr. Guy-Smith, the Prosecution seeks to tender the CV and report of Mr. Treanor into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We would object to the admission of Mr. Treanor's report. We have no objection to the admission of Mr. Treanor's CV. I don't know if you wish for me to go any further at this time. At this time we would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether it's you or her who should start, but certainly the Trial Chamber would like to know your reasons for objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, they are many. Initially, to the extent the report renders any opinions, as has been previously argued in our submissions concerning our initial objections to Mr. Treanor's reports, what we essentially have at this time is an individual who has read a great deal of information, but his opinions, I believe through the examination specifically as they related to his report, reveal that they are, one, not well-founded, and by that I mean that his methodology for purposes of this report is pretty much non-existent. The criteria that he used for making a determination of what information he would present to the Chamber as being relevant is hidden. He testified at least twice that it was contained within the recesses of his own mind. And I may be paraphrasing his exact language, but there is no objective information upon which the Chamber can rely concerning what he believed to be important or not important. He is rendering an opinion in much the same way that I could render an opinion. I could tell you precisely what I think of what the situation would be. And I may well be right, I may well be wrong, but in the absence of some objective basis upon which the Chamber could rely, it would be imprudent in our submission to place any emphasis on such opinions. To the extent that he has given you factual information, it's clear that once again he engaged in a process of distinguishing and delineating, based upon a series of criteria which we have no information about. We don't know why he gave us certain information and not other information. It's clear that he has contradicted himself with regard to the importance that he attributed to the involvement of international organisations and international personages with regard to how it impacted upon his determination of what would be included in the report or not. It is clear that also his report, as he candidly stated - as a matter of fact, he brought it up - is directed towards something that apparently he was not even, from what we've been told, asked to do, which is to facilitate, as he put it - I'm referring to paragraph 5 of his introduction - "a realistic and accurate understanding of a larger context in which it is alleged that the Serbian leadership was involved in massive violations of humanitarian law in BH and Croatia," which apparently was something he told us was not discussed at the meeting that he had with Ms. Somers and I believe Mr. Ossogo. He took it upon himself to slant, colour, or put the report in a particular light. So he definitely was not giving us from the outset an objective, balanced information upon which you can make a determination, and by that I mean -- and I'm not suggesting you can't distinguish and delineate yourselves, but rather the manner in which he is suggesting you should engage in this analysis of value-neutral facts. He really is, when all is said and done, a summary witness. What he's done is he's compiled a fair number of facts. He's done it in an arbitrary fashion, as I've just mentioned, and he's put them together so that you have a summary of the events that occurred during the period of time. But to the extent this report is to concern itself with the Bosnian leadership for the period of time identified, 1990 to 1995, even to the extent he is a summary witness, it is spotty, it is incomplete, it is clearly slanted, and I would go so far as to say biased. And I'm not attributing any reason for that bias to exist because I, quite frankly, don't know why it does exist. I'm not suggesting that his employment and his employment alone would have any impact. However, I think he quite candidly has established the failures of his own analysis in his testimony as it relates to his report. I would submit that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on the question of bias, those questions should have been put to Mr. Treanor in cross-examination, in my submission. Further, the report is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought she was looking at me meaningfully. I am more than happy to respond at an appropriate time. I'm not going to jump up. I had a feeling she wanted an answer from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. You will stand up when you have to reply, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report is not spotty; it's not incomplete. Your Honour will see that from the report Mr. Treanor has diligently taken all of the facts and not simply about the -- in order to show the goals of the Serb leadership, he also in his report makes reference to what the other parties were doing during the whole of the time of the conflict. An expert's task, Your Honour, is to identify issues, analyse them, and associate them, and they can tell consistency and contradictions between other documents and recognise connections where other people may miss them. And it's through his 14 years of analysing the documentary collections that are within the OTP that have given him this in-depth knowledge of the conflict. And he has told you on numerous occasions in questions put by the Bench and by the Defence that he has picked the most important documents. He's also distinguished between, for example, the weight that he gives a Security Council resolution as opposed to a letter from the Secretary-General; that was this morning. But he's condensed hundreds and hundreds of documents into a 75-page report and into a form that can communicate, you know, the concepts that the report is about succinctly for the trier of fact. And it's my submission, Your Honour, that this report will assist Your Honours because if Your Honours were to review the underlying documentation which is footnoted to the report and, in my view, there's no doubt that for an expert opinion to have any value, that the facts on which it's based must be before the Court so that you can judge for yourself whether -- whether, in fact, Mr. Treanor has done a complete analysis and a complete job. Mr. Treanor said to you at - sorry, Your Honour - page 1281 of the transcript that he chose the ones that were, in his estimation, the most relevant, and he does that from a period of 14 years of analysis of these document collections. Also, in answer to a question in cross-examination, he was satisfied that the report was as accurate and as complete as possible. Your Honour, we submit that the report should be admitted. Mr. Treanor does have the expertise to render this report. And those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, you say that the job of an expert is to identify issues, analyse them and associate them and establish the consistency between documents and recognise connections where others may miss them. Is that what is said to be the job of an expert in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, or is it that the expert must be able, through application of his expert knowledge, to analyse issues that are in dispute between the parties to enable the Bench to make a determination on those issues, something to that effect? I'm paraphrasing here. I'm not quite -- I can try and say it a little more clearly. An expert is a person who, by virtue of some specialised knowledge, skill or training, can assist the trier of fact to understand or determine an issue in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My -- I have a problem, a number of problems, actually. First of all, you'll recall that on the very first day of Mr. Treanor's testimony, while you were qualifying him as an expert, he clearly said to you that he had no methodology that he applied in collecting his evidence; that he used his personal opinion, not expert opinion and that he was virtually expressing his own personal opinions, and that question of expressing --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told that the accused and everyone else listening through the B/C/S channel is not receiving interpretation. Is that a fact? Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just received the sound again on this channel, but I'm sorry, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not receiving the interpretation of what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You have to be tuned in to channel 4 to receive English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am now on channel 4, ma'am. You will remember we went to channel 0 when we had problems earlier in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we can hear the Serbian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. I was still saying that he clearly, in his own words, said he was expressing his own personal opinions, he had no methodology, and he had no criteria that he employed in choosing the information that he put before us. Now, I would expect that an expert witness should have certain professional criteria that he uses which we laypeople -- that's why he's called to come here, because he's come to unravel things that in which we are lay, saying them in simple terms and using his professional expertise and, at the end of it all, to give us his professional opinion on all those facts that he has unravelled. And I am not aware of you, Madam Sutherland, asking the witness at the end of his testimony in chief, or at any stage, to provide us with any professional opinion based upon the facts that he testified on. I'm not aware of that opinion being given through cross-examination. So I have these problems when it comes to qualification of Mr. Treanor as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, he may not have articulated it as well as he could, but he did say that of all the documents that he reviewed, he took the most important ones. And if I can take Your Honour to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is the most important ones and the most relevant ones that you mentioned a little earlier. How does he determine that? That importance and that relevance can only come out and be demonstrated to the Chamber against the criteria that he uses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can take you to paragraph 6 of the introduction of the report, and it says that "the report is based primarily on available records of the Serbian entities concerned and international organisations, especially important sources are Official Gazettes and the minutes or transcripts of sessions of the Serbian official bodies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does he determine importance, ma'am? That's my question. His professional expertise must help -- he must give us his criteria from his professional perspective and tell us how he determines that this is important, that is not important. Again, he told us here that for those kind of decisions, he used his personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But his personal opinion based on 14 years of experience of reviewing massive document collections, and he says that the sources have been supplemented by a few press reports and other media items that directly report on them, and sparing use has been made of memoirs and similar literature. So he has told you the importance of what -- what he places as the most important documents, and they are the SDC minutes, the RS -- the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions. So he is saying to you that, I picked the most important documents, i.e., the ones that are Official Gazettes and minutes of the transcript of sessions of the Serbian official bodies. So this report isn't footnoted by -- I mean, there are some newspaper articles referenced in -- cited in this report, but you will see from the underlying documentation, that the underlying documentation is what is stated in paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He says: "In other words, this report draws almost exclusively on the contemporaneous documentary record, most of it created by the Serb leaders themselves."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And these documents could have been collected by anybody. You could have done it; I could have done it, without being a historian, because no criteria are required except to say what is important and what I, as a person, think is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What he's done is analysed all of these documents and then succinctly put it into the 75-page report for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Precisely what the Defence is saying: He's a summary witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that conclusions can be gleaned from every paragraph of the report. I mean, he's saying that there's no conclusion in the report, but the whole -- the whole issue for him is that an ordinary person can't do what he's done. I mean, he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is it that he did that an ordinary person can't do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He's taken a large number of documents and reviewed them and analysed them and then put them into context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you can't do that? You? When you studied at university on a particular subject, you read various textbooks related to the topic, and when you sat in the exam, you condensed all that information and put it down into pages that you can write in three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So does that make you an expert?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, because I've been -- you know, I mean, the example you use, Your Honour, is you're doing a subject for either six months or 12 months of a year. Mr. Treanor has been looking at these documents for 14 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. He had two years to look at -- to do this specific job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, he -- Your Honour, he had six weeks, from August 2000 until the middle of -- I think the first report is dated the 10th of October, 2006. It was then filed with the Court over the ensuing two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He then went back to the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Refined it again in September, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- and then modified it slightly, fixing up all the ERN numbers, and he was asked, Was this an accurate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not contesting the accuracy, ma'am. I'm just contesting his qualifications. I'm not even contesting. I would like you to address the Chamber, and I'm saying this because the questions I'm raising with you came from his own mouth. He told us here that he's doing this from his personal opinions. He has no criteria; he has no methodology; he has nothing. And I'm not convinced that anybody can't do that, anybody can't summarize a hundred pages into two pages, 31.000 pages into 75 pages, if you want to do that. Anyway, we're five minutes beyond the break. I see you've got a note. Look at the note. Let's carry on after the break. Come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Judge David has some questions to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mrs. Sutherland, as I understand from the introduction, the expert, in paragraph 5, said, "the primary purpose of such a description ..." What gives me to understand that this is a descriptive study, and you know as studies could be divided in various categories; for instance, a study requiring verification, which are studies that involve a hypothesis of some kind that has to verify through explanation and verification. This is not a study to verify a hypothesis. It is a descriptive study. First point, do you agree that this is a descriptive study in general?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In paragraph 4 he says: "The aim of the report is to describe and document some of the events of particular importance."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Very well. It's a descriptive study. Second, what are the main parameters that in paragraph (a) of 5 he says. "Facilitate a realistic ..." What is "real"? I will not go into the discussion of the word, but "real" it is something that describes the reality of events. And second, he said accurate. So this study intends to portray in a most reliable way what understanding? What is the word "understanding"? I am not going to go into philology here, but the origin of the word is a word, in German, "philosophie verstand." In "verstand," understanding, implies all the capture of the meaning of a given situation. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Fine. Third point. He says that larger context in which it is alleged that the "Serbian leadership was involved in massive violations of international humanitarian law in BH in Croatia." So here, in this paragraph, it seems that the expert report tries to link the understanding with legal elements of humanitarian law, because he said "Serbian leadership involving massive violations of international humanitarian in BH and Croatia." Are you in agreement with me, that this paragraph links factual situations to the purpose of a legal dimension?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as it's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Third, (b), "to identify the individuals who fill the highest level military and civilian positions within the Serbian entities." Are you in agreement that the expert has done efforts in order to identify the individuals?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Give me examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report is replete with the names of the highest level civilian and military leaders in the three entities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, the report says it's "based primarily on available records of Serbian entities concerned and international organisations primarily the UN. Especially important sources are Official Gazettes and the minutes or transcripts of sessions of Serbian official bodies." Could you give me examples in the report in which available records and Official Gazettes and minutes are expressed in the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Give me some.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Paragraphs, for example, 66: "The Bosnian Serb Assembly held a 4th session." 69: "The 5th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly." 68: "The 9th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly." 71: "The 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I am just trying to test the purpose of the report, asking you some questions, because I didn't want to examine the witness because I didn't want to give to him so heavy a burden at this moment because in many instances, even though he has reaffirmed the objective line of his analysis and descriptive studies, in some moments, due to the confusion of the questions, he came with selections of the inner recessions of the mind, which is absolutely contrary to what he has done in quoting the answer, and we could not take this small phrase as directing the whole heavy weight of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, Your Honour. If we could go to page 100 -- page 85 of the report, and it lists all of the sources. And you can see by going down the page what the sources are: UN resolutions, UN resolutions, report -- Badinter reports, laws on the army, constitutions, statements by the -- by the parties, proclamations, decisions, the Assembly, the Serbian Defence Council minutes, the SFRY Presidency transcripts, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland, thank you very much. Another question. Are you in agreement with me that the purpose of the study as it's presented is not the whole story of the situation? And he said: "The focus is rather on the goal is much less a history said of the whole or any part of the former Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree, but within the -- within the report that he has given, he does make note of what is happening at the time in relation to the other actors, the other parties, the Muslims and the Croats, and the international community. That is replete all the way through the report, as well as identifying on the main aim of the report and that is the Serb -- the goals of the Serbian leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: In one of the early questions I put to him, two days ago I believe, I asked him who gave him the goals of the study and he answered, It was the Prosecution. Are you in agreement with the answer? I asked him, Who gave you the goals of the Prosecution? And he said, I was given by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and he said that again in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: How do the goals of the Prosecution in this study, I would like you to elaborate, have impacted on the objective selection of the elements that he presented? Could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I think he said in cross-examination that he actually went broader than his remit. His remit was, by the Prosecution, to submit a report on the goals of the Serbian leadership. And I think this goes to show how unbiased he is, because he's, in fact, said, This is what I've been asked to do, but I think I need to also include this and this and this in my report because I think it's relevant to the question that I've been asked and the brief that I've been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So in many ways you are telling us that the initial commitment has been, in many ways, overcome in the sense of limitations for a given purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. I have no more questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith, I guess you're entitled to a reply, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The only reason that I'm hesitating here for a moment is I'm reflecting upon the questions that have been presented by the Bench, by both of Your Honours, and seeing whether or not based on those questions I think there's any further explanation that needs to be made or any further submissions that need to be made. And I think, really quite briefly and just quickly, with regard to the issue of bias, bias is not necessarily something which is explained through cross-examination. Bias is oftentimes self-evident and needs no further inquiry. With regard to that particular issue, I don't believe there's any further necessity for an imposition upon any party, be it the Prosecution or the Defence, to further examine the issue of bias if one is manifest or if a party believes it's manifest, one can argue off the facts that have been presented. It's obviously up to the trier of fact to make a determination of whether or not that's an accurate perception or an inaccurate perception, and I leave it at that. One of the things that's been said here, and it's been said repeatedly, actually, it's a form of -- criticised as a form of logical argument and the Prosecution's argument, quite simply put, is circular in its reasoning, which is because he said it was important, it is important; because he has spent a long period of time analysing or reviewing a particular area, therefore it must be important because he says it is important. Well, that's a logical fallacy. It's a recognised logical fallacy, and I believe that the -- that the Chamber has rightfully and rightly identified one of the major problems that exists here, which is that, in fact, his information is that of a summary witness. And whether it be called descriptive or it has an objective hypothesis, his report remains the same. And to the extent that that can be of assistance to you, I question -- it's our submission, I question whether or not it's of any assistance to you because, in fact, any one of us could have done the exact same thing, which is review a body of documents, make a determination based on that body of documents that we believe to be important, educated ourselves in the field, and submitted a body of documents which then would be presented to you for purposes of analysis. Now, I can do that. If you give me -- if you give me 60 days or even more so, two years, I promise you I will write a report within 60 pages that contains a great deal of information, that is predicated on the precise documents that you have in front of you. It would include documents that you do not have in front of you, documents which apparently were not taken into account, I am sure. But ultimately, had I been -- had I done such a thing and was I in such a position, I would be rightfully criticised for doing the precise thing which we suggest is occurring here, which is rendering my personal opinion about the state of affairs and summarizing a series of documents in a different formation. That's not what an expert's for. That's not why an expert should be presented to you, nor should their report be presented to you. There's another problem here which is that Mr. Treanor, who has acknowledged that he is not a lawyer, according to his introduction, has apparently, at least internally and maybe externally, clearly overstepped the bounds with regard to what his internal determination would be of violations of international humanitarian law. And that certainly is an area in which he would be violating the boundaries of the function of the fact-finding process and substituting his own personal opinion for that of the fact-finder, which, in our respectful submission, is you, the Chamber. Once again, we don't deviate from the position that was initially made, which is that we object to the admission of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. The Chamber will sleep over it and come up with a decision later. Thank you very much. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be led by Mr. Rafael La Cruz, and I would ask that I may be excused, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused, ma'am. Mr. La Cruz.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. La Cruz will take a moment to rearrange the furniture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: The Prosecution would call witness Branko Bubenik, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Branko Bubenik. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I believe your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, we advised the Trial Chamber and the Defence the week before last that Dr. Branko Bubenik will be called viva voce. He was originally listed as 92 ter witness, but the Prosecution will conduct its examination-in-chief within the same estimated time of 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. La Cruz.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Are you sitting comfortable, witness?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: My name is Branko Bubenik, and I was born on the 18th of April, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I'm currently retired, and I'm still involved in the affairs that I used to be involved in in the past, but this time as a freelancer, as a consultant for document management in their analogue and digital forms, and also as a consultant for the Croatian parliament, and digitalised TV system. And I feel quite fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: What was your occupation back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: At that time I was the Director of the Information and Documentation Centre, or, rather, that department, including the archives of the Croatian Television, which was part of the Croatian Radio and Television Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: What is the acronym for that company?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: The Croatian Radio and Television. In other words, it includes both the radio broadcasting company, and the television. So the acronym is HRT.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: What was your position in HRT?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, I was the head of a work unit which included -- I supervised about 80 employees. This was a multi-media logistical service for the television journalists, but we also served the radio journalists in preparing documentation for them. And I was among the five highest managers. My official post was the Director of the Production Department of the TV, and I was on the board of the television company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I remained in that position until 2005, when I retired, and I was appointed as the head of this centre, the documentation centre, in 1974. In other words, I spent many years, over 30 years, in this field. And before that I worked as a journalist and a reporter, a film reporter, beginning in 1963. In other words, I spent 41 years working for the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: And besides your work in HRT as head of the information department and archives, have you completed studies in that field, in the field of archiving and audiovisual material?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Well, I did various jobs. I began my studies as a chemical technician and then I started working in the film industry as an amateur. And it's paradoxical then that I started my study and I actually completed the school for camera broadcasting, and I was appointed as the head of these archives, although I was a very young man. And to everyone's surprise, and everybody kept asking me, Are you mad? Why did you accept this post? And I said, Well, I want to look after my kids. So I took care of both my own films and also the films of my colleagues. As for the question that you asked, I was not really fully qualified for this job, but I had a lot of knowledge about film. And then I enrolled in graduate studies in the field of information studies, and in 1974 I received my master's degree in this field, and ten years ago I received a Ph.D. at the School of Philosophy. My thesis was entitled -- dealt with the digitalisation of audiovisual media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: And throughout this career, have you been member -- are you member of various professional associations that relates to this area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes. As early as 1974 I realised that we were very ignorant in this field, and I immediately set up, together with my colleagues, an organisation of -- which united eight Yugoslav radio and television archives under one umbrella. This was a unique organisation of its type in Europe at the time, and I was president of that association until the breakup of Yugoslavia. I was also its representative in the UNESCO, as a representative of the Yugoslav Radio Television. And all the Yugoslav media centres and documentation centres, through my office, became members of an international organisation, the International Federation of TV Archives, which numbers about 220 members. At first I was coordinator for Balkan states. Then I became coordinator for central Europe, following which I became a member of the executive board of that organisation and its vice-president. I was also a candidate for its president, but I was elected vice-president, and for eight years I was a president of the Professional Trade Commission. And I still am very active in this area. I organise seminars and workshops throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Dr. Bubenik, back in 1995, did you meet with the ICTY representatives in around June that year, more specifically a representative from the Office of the Prosecutor, or OTP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: At the time did you provide these representatives with any material, any sort of material?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: We provided about 200 video documents to this Tribunal. The documentation was relayed through the documentation service in Zagreb and I was given the assignment by my director. Our office received support from the government and the government ordered the Supreme Court to create an office for cooperation with the Tribunal, and Mr. Vukovic, who at this time was the Chief Justice, received from my director, Mr. Vrdoljak, or, rather, my director appointed me to be the point man and the responsible person for bringing this programme into reality. Most of these documents were oral documents. We frequently had occasion to deal with investigators of this Office of the Prosecutor. We provided them access to our database by creating a broad selection of documents, allowing them to search through this database and review the video documentation. And once they made their selection, we provided -- we made copies and lists of these documents and the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor took over these documents, together with the lists, while my responsibility was to provide this list of documents that had been handed over to the Tribunal to my director. And this worked pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: And amongst this material that you provided to the OTP representatives, did you also provide a copy of a videotape related to the events of the shelling of the city of Zagreb of 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: With respect to this copy of a videotape or footage, who was the provider of this videotape? More clearly, how did HRT receive or got that videotape?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: We could not answer that question immediately. In our database we do not have all the details that should be there, and upon the insistence of the investigators, we conducted an investigation. I have to say that we were lucky. We found in another service, not the archives department but in the Service for International Exchanges, we found a fax that we had received from Brussels, or, rather, that service had received from Brussels, from the Eurovision Exchange Department and all the information was contained therein. I suppose that this fax is in the possession of this Court. It can be seen there that this document had been sent from Brussels.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is asked to repeat the last part of his sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: I would like to ask you again: From who did HRT receive or got that videotape? More specifically, who was the provider of this videotape to HRT?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: As I already mentioned, we received this through a system of exchange. First of all, I'll tell you how we received it in the archives. The procedure is the following: Every programme, once it was broadcast, would have to be handed over to the archives, and this was a major feat during the war, but we managed to work in this way. Now, this videotape was recorded on two videotapes, Betacam. One of them was shown on the main news programme of that day at 7.30 p.m., and the other Betacam cassette was archived because this had been shown at the end of a programme called "Picture Against Picture." The originals of these -- the originals of these recorded programmes are in the archives, but we made copies. Now, we received -- although that's not my job, we received this from Brussels from the Eurovision exchange department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: You answered your question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. La Cruz, I'll ask you to control your witness. We haven't got much time. And if you can get him to be precise and to the point. You asked him who provided, and he tells you how he provided. You should have stopped him at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: When is it that you received a copy of this video footage that we're talking about, on what date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I can't tell you off the cuff, but it can be established. There are documents to that effect. This was 13 years ago. It was on the same day when this event took place, or, rather, when this was broadcast. I think it was on the 2nd of May, on the same day of the actual event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: With respect to this copy of the video, I would like to ask you: From who is the Eurovision got the copy of the video? From which broadcaster, as you have explained, Eurovision received --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, from the fax it can be concluded that Eurovision had received that through their exchange from the Yugoslav Radio and Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: What is the acronym for this company, the Yugoslav Radio and Television, that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you for certain, but you can find it in the fax that I mentioned earlier. I think YURTS, or URTS. Yugoslav Radio and Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Okay. Where this YURTS was based physically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I would like to move, and I'd like to play a video-clip that has been taken from the exhibit 65 ter number 01387. This tape or clip has been synchronised with the transcript in English and copies of the transcript in English have been provided to the interpreters. So I would like the English transcript be read into the record while the video-clip is played. It has a duration of around two minutes and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to place on the record that the video is going to start at 00:00:48:7?

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "MILAN MARTIC: Dear brothers and sisters, Your Eminence. I wish to address a few words to you and tell you about the situation that has befallen us and about what we plan to do next to get out of all this. First of all, I want to tell you that I sincerely sympathise with all the suffering that you've endured. I would have preferred the situation to be good and that I'd come to attend a wedding in Western Slavonia, rather than having to come here when you're in your darkest hour to explain how to get out of this and how to find a way out of all this so that you don't wander around and so that we keep our land. We've had a meeting here with the civilian authorities, the military leadership, and our archpriests. What Croatia has done to us is undoubtedly a crime which was supported by foreign powers: America and Germany. This was not a matter of treason; it is solely that our enemy had the upper hand at the moment and managed to take control of the motorway and of this part, as you know. But I'm telling you this: One lost battle doesn't mean that the war has been lost. As a countermeasure to what Tudjman did to you here, we have shelled all their cities: Sisak several times, Karlovac, Zagreb, both yesterday and today. This was done for you. But let me tell you that the attack by Tudjman's forces did not focus only on Western Slavonia only; he also attacked Lika and Dalmatia. Lika managed to defend itself, and in Dalmatia their forces were removed from Mount Dinara. Today, an ultimatum followed: If they continued to attack our besieged forces, we would continue to pound Zagreb and destroy their cities. They then begged us to stop shelling Zagreb and said that they'd let our people out of the encirclement, which is what interests you the most."

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Dr. Bubenik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you ask the next question, what do you want to do with that videotape?

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: In the end I would like to be -- introduce it into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Is this clip that we have played a copy of the footage that HRT received on the 3rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes, it is a copy from the programme -- from the news programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: And would it be accurate to say that this is a copy which is the same that was given to the OTP representatives in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly refer to us who appears talking on the tape?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Well, you all know it very well. That man is Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Dr. Bubenik, after HRT received this video, was this video broadcast?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I do not understand your question. Was it broadcast? Yes, of course, it was broadcast on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: What day it was? If you say that it was broadcast on the same day, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you for certain because I don't have in front of me the paper that I gave you, but I was on the same day when Zagreb was shelled and on the same day when he made the statement. I'm not a historian, and dates are not my strong suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, where was this video broadcast?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I mentioned that as well. It was broadcast for the first time in a major news programme which is called "The Television Dnevnik" at 7:30 p.m., and then it was re-broadcast in a programme called "Slika na Sliku," and subsequently every year on the date on the anniversary, it is re-broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, then, that it was broadcast in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: And do you know where else, apart from Croatia, was this video broadcast?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: No. At the time there were no rival television channels yet. I'm not sure if OTV, another channel, broadcast it. Probably, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have a word with my colleague for a minute, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Dr. Bubenik, with respect to the broadcast, was this video broadcast outside Croatia by any other company, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: I can't claim that with any certainty, but it was a very important event. It must have been rebroadcast. And the Eurovision centre in Brussels must have records of that. They know exactly which countries took over the footage when it was offered. I'm pretty sure, by the way, that Slovenia and the neighbouring countries of Serbia did take it. I can't be sure, but it would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like this video-clip to be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video-clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Could you give us the 65 ter number of this video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: 01387, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: I want to make clear, as I said before, that this is a portion of 01387. The original version is longer. This is just the minutes that we talked about before. It's just the beginning. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination? I see, Mr. Lukic, you standing forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope this microphone is working now and you can hear me, as well as the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bubenik, good afternoon. My name is Novak Lukic, and on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Perisic, I'll be questioning you briefly. From what I heard today in direct examination, some things were new to me and that's why I'd like to ask you a few questions. You said you were a member of the board of the Croatian Television.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: No. It's called the board of management. We didn't have any authority. The actual power was at the level of the RTV. We were just managing the day-to-day business of the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever attend collegium meetings of editorial boards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, or do you know from what time was the broadcasting of television of Serbia available in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: No. We had a problem, and you know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: No. I was surprised. For instance, concerning Vukovar, we had a lot of material of Serbian origin because we didn't have contact then, but the archive is full of material. The broadcasting reached them, obviously. I'm surprised, and it could really be analysed, but we have materials from Republika Srpska in the archives. That material and the investigation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the question. We had a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want the witness to repeat the question or the answer? Madam Interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes what?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a moment before you start answering. Concerning this answer, would you just clear up, in response to the question from the Prosecution, you said a moment ago that the source of that footage was Radio Television Serbia, that is URTS, as you saw in the fax message forwarded to you from Brussels.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in your 1995 statement, you went a bit further and said in the documentation you saw the name of the real author and the real source of that footage. So based on the documents that you personally have seen, how did you identify the author of the original footage and the channel by which it reached you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: You are now referring me to documents you have in your hand and I don't. Let me see it. I came here empty-handed. I don't know. I don't remember. But it's not only my interpretation. The document is in English. The investigators have seen this. It says -- there is a name of the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read from your statement. I didn't mean to tender this document or put it to you, but you said in your statement, and I'm reading the B/C/S version: "We received this footage from the Eurovision Exchange Department and a European association of broadcasters, and they received it from Broadcasting Station Yugoslavia radio and Television Serbia," in parenthesis, "(YURTS) who, in turn, received it from a London News Company called GBWTN, who had the footage first." That's what you said. Does this refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: You see, I said clearly that WTN should be asked. They still exist, and I believe the Prosecution investigators paid them a visit. They produced the document. They were on the spot. Whether they had been to Banja Luka or Belgrade, I don't know. I am a television person. To me it doesn't matter. But Belgrade sent it to Brussels, that's for sure, or perhaps the records in Brussels are bad. It's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll appreciate short answers, please. As a man who spent many years working in the television business, would you agree that in the broader period, let's say 1990 onwards through end of 1995, the authorities had a very strong influence on the media.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: Yes, like everywhere, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether in the period we're discussing - and I'm interested particularly in 1995 - you had an official exchange of programmes with the Television of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: It was not within my purview, but I can tell you that I had a very good relationship before the war, and I still have it today, with my colleagues Mr. Kecina, and it's in the archives. You should ask him. He should have it. And the name is Kecina. I want to correct the interpreters. Kecina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- strike that. A moment ago, in responding to the Prosecutor, you said you had a very good cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY, and you gave them over 200 documents, if I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: 236 or something. 186.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they address you with requests for material concerning Ante Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BUBENIK
utterances.text: No. I was out of the business by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Any re-examination, Mr. La Cruz?

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Bubenik, thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. This brings us to the end of your testimony, and you are now excused. You may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon, I saw your colleague Mr. La Cruz also stood up simultaneously with you, but he deferred to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. La Cruz could be excused at this point so he can say goodbye to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does he want to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LA CRUZ
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the time we have left today, prior to the start of the testimony of Mr. Torkildsen, there are a few points that I would simply like to put on the record and explain to the Trial Chamber. As the Chamber knows, Mr. Torkildsen first wrote his report -- well, he wrote his report in November 2002 and the present report that is being studied in this case contains no substantive changes in the text. Simply, the Prosecution has simply replaced the 65 ter numbers that related to the Slobodan Milosevic proceedings in 2002 with the 65 ter numbers that relate to these proceedings. Having said that, yesterday I realised that while I was switching 65 ter numbers in this process, I made two mistakes which I would like to bring to your attention. The first is the bottom of page 22, paragraph 62, the 65 ter number should say "6530" and not "B3501," as it presently says. Secondly, Your Honour, at paragraph 118, the bottom of page 43, the 65 ter number should be 532, not 523. Your Honours, the Prosecution has decided that it will not rely on the following paragraphs in Mr. Torkildsen's report: 23 and 79 through 83.
